final_proof:
The claim is false as written. Indeed, even in the real Banach space V = ℝ, let I = J = K = ℕ₀, let v₀ = 1 and vᵢ = 0 for every i ≥ 1, and take r = 1. Define the first enumeration by jₙ = n, and define the second by k₀ = 1, k₁ = 0, and kₙ = n for n ≥ 2. Then ∑_{n=1}^∞ v_{jₙ} = 0, so the series on the left does not converge to r, whereas ∑_{n=1}^∞ v_{kₙ} = 1 and this series is absolutely convergent. Thus the displayed equivalence fails because the sums begin at 1 and consequently omit j₀ and k₀, which need not represent the same index. There is also a type issue: for an arbitrary Banach space V, a positive real number r is not necessarily an element of V, so convergence of a V-valued series to r need not be meaningful.

A natural corrected statement is the following. Let x ∈ V, and let both series begin at n = 0. Then

∑_{n=0}^∞ v_{jₙ} converges absolutely to x if and only if ∑_{n=0}^∞ v_{kₙ} converges absolutely to x.

Proof of the corrected statement. Put S = {i ∈ I : vᵢ ≠ 0}. By hypothesis, S ⊆ J ∩ K. Suppose first that ∑_{n=0}^∞ v_{jₙ} converges absolutely to x. Thus ∑_{n=0}^∞ ‖v_{jₙ}‖ is finite and the partial sums ∑_{n=0}^N v_{jₙ} tend to x.

First we prove absolute convergence in the k-enumeration. For any m, discard from {k₀,…,kₘ} the indices outside S; their corresponding vectors are zero. The remaining indices form a finite subset of S. Every one of them occurs exactly once in the enumeration (jₙ), so

∑_{q=0}^m ‖v_{k_q}‖ ≤ ∑_{n=0}^∞ ‖v_{jₙ}‖.

The partial sums on the left are nondecreasing and bounded, and hence ∑_{q=0}^∞ ‖v_{k_q}‖ converges. Therefore the k-series is absolutely convergent.

It remains to identify its sum. Let ε > 0. Choose N such that

‖x − ∑_{n=0}^N v_{jₙ}‖ < ε/2    and    ∑_{n=N+1}^∞ ‖v_{jₙ}‖ < ε/2.

Let A = S ∩ {j₀,…,j_N}. This is a finite subset of K. Since (kₙ) enumerates K, there is M such that A ⊆ {k₀,…,k_M}. For every m ≥ M, all the nonzero terms among v_{j₀},…,v_{j_N} occur in ∑_{q=0}^m v_{k_q}. All its other nonzero terms have indices in S ∖ A, and hence occur in the j-enumeration only after position N. Consequently, for some finite set F_m ⊆ {N+1,N+2,…},

∑_{q=0}^m v_{k_q} − ∑_{n=0}^N v_{jₙ} = ∑_{n∈F_m} v_{jₙ}.

(The order of this finite sum is immaterial.) By the triangle inequality,

‖∑_{q=0}^m v_{k_q} − x‖ ≤ ‖∑_{q=0}^m v_{k_q} − ∑_{n=0}^N v_{jₙ}‖ + ‖∑_{n=0}^N v_{jₙ} − x‖ ≤ ∑_{n=N+1}^∞ ‖v_{jₙ}‖ + ε/2 < ε.

Thus the k-partial sums tend to x. This proves that the k-series converges absolutely to x. The reverse implication follows by the identical argument with j and k interchanged, proving the corrected equivalence.

If the intended role of the positive real r was instead to denote the absolute mass, the corresponding type-correct formulation is ∑_{n=0}^∞ ‖v_{jₙ}‖ = r if and only if ∑_{n=0}^∞ ‖v_{kₙ}‖ = r. This also follows from the proof: applying the displayed finite-subset bound in both directions shows that the two nonnegative series have the same sum.
